title: Fitting ear tags on sheep
subtitle: UK law requires all sheep to carry two ear tags before they leave the holding where they were born. The timing, tag type, and record are all specified.
excerpt: Sheep in the UK must be tagged with two approved ear tags, both carrying the flock mark and individual number, before they move off their birth holding. Lambs born for breeding must be tagged within 9 months; lambs going to slaughter before 12 months only need a slaughter tag. Here is the legal position, the equipment, and the technique.
sourceNotes: DEFRA, Sheep and Goat Identification, Traceability and Registration (SI 2021/1370), current regulations. Rural Payments Agency (RPA) sheep identification guidance leaflet. APHA livestock traceability guidance.

glossaryTerms.definition: A unique 4-letter code allocated to each registered flock, prefixed to each animal's individual number on the ear tag. Example: ABCD1234. Applied for by the flock keeper from APHA after the CPH number is issued.

A purpose-made tool resembling a pair of pliers that holds the tag and pin and punches them through the ear in one clean movement. Tag-specific: each manufacturer's tag requires the matching applicator.

content.text: UK sheep identification law requires two tags per animal. At minimum: one electronic tag (EID) in one ear and one conventional tag carrying the same
and number in the other ear. Both tags must be applied before the animal moves off the birth holding for any reason.
Your flock mark, applied for from APHA after your CPH is issued. Without a flock mark, the tags cannot be ordered.
Approved UK sheep tags from a registered supplier. Tags must meet UK-approved EID standards. Order in advance, suppliers print the flock mark and sequence number on each tag.
from the same supplier as the tags.
Your flock register, to record the tag number and date of tagging for each animal.

The tag goes in the middle third of the ear, between the large blood vessel running along the top of the ear and the cartilage ridge at the lower edge. Avoid the top blood vessel, a tag through this causes significant bleeding and a tag that stays loose. Avoid the very base of the ear, the skin is very thick there and the tag may not seat correctly.
Load the applicator: male (pin) side of the tag in the bottom jaw, female (receiver) side in the top jaw.
Hold the lamb's head firmly with your free arm. Locate the tag site with your finger.

Place the applicator jaws either side of the ear at the chosen site, avoiding the blood vessel. Close the applicator in one smooth, firm movement. A hesitant partial close leaves the tag loose; a full close seats it cleanly.
Check the tag is seated: it should not rotate freely and the pin should not visible be protruding on one side.
Record the tag number in the flock register with the date of tagging and the animal's dam (mother) where known.

When a sheep loses a tag, it must be replaced within 28 days and before it moves off the holding. The replacement tag carries the same number as the lost one (not a new number) and is recorded in the flock register. Order replacement tags from your supplier specifying the exact number to be duplicated.
